opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions for a team like ours, and I'd say the short answer is that physician expertise can't be something you bolt on at the end. It has to be woven in from the very beginning.

When I think about how we approach health, there are a few layers where clinical expertise really matters. The first is just defining what "good" looks like. It's very easy as an AI researcher to optimize for something that looks reasonable on paper, like accuracy on a multiple-choice medical exam, and those benchmarks were useful for a while, but they don't capture what actually matters in a real clinical interaction. Physicians are the ones who can tell you: this answer is technically correct but would confuse a patient, or this response misses the one follow-up question any good doctor would ask, or this is fine for a clinician audience but dangerous for a layperson. So a lot of the work is having physicians help us design evaluations and rubrics that reflect real-world quality, things like whether the model escalates appropriately, whether it hedges where there's genuine uncertainty, whether it communicates in a way that's actually helpful.

The second layer is in the data and the feedback itself. When you're training models, the judgments you're encoding matter enormously, and in health those judgments should come from people with deep clinical experience, and ideally from a diverse set of them: different specialties, different practice settings, different countries. Medicine isn't monolithic. What's standard of care in one setting may not be accessible in another, and we want models that are useful for people all over the world, not just in a well-resourced academic hospital.

And then the third layer, which I think is underrated, is having physicians embedded on the team as real collaborators rather than as consultants you call in occasionally. Some of the best insights come from informal conversations, a clinician looking over a researcher's shoulder and saying, "Actually, that's not how this works in practice." You want that tight feedback loop. I've found the most productive setups are ones where clinicians and ML researchers develop a shared language, where the researchers understand enough medicine to ask good questions and the physicians understand enough about how models are trained to know where their input has the most leverage.

The other thing I'd add is a bit of humility in both directions. Physicians bring irreplaceable judgment, but they also disagree with each other a lot, and part of the research challenge is figuring out how to handle that disagreement productively rather than pretending there's always one right answer. So integrating physician expertise isn't just about deference; it's about building processes where that expertise is captured carefully, debated, and translated into something the model can actually learn from.

Ultimately the goal is models that people, and clinicians, can genuinely trust, and you just can't get there without doctors deeply involved in shaping them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says physicians should be embedded as real collaborators, not consulted only occasionally, and describes an ongoing feedback loop with researchers.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions input from a diverse set of physicians, but does not describe close physician advisers synthesizing broader physician-community input for the team.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that physicians can't be a consultation layer bolted onto the end of the research process. They have to be in the room from the start, and ideally some of them have to be researchers themselves.

Let me explain why I feel so strongly about that. When I was working on Med-PaLM at Google, one of the biggest lessons was that the hard part of medical AI isn't getting a model to answer board exam questions. The hard part is defining what "good" even means. A response can be factually correct and still be dangerous because it's missing a key caveat, or it fails to escalate when it should, or it reads as confident in a way that a worried patient at two in the morning shouldn't take at face value. Figuring out those dimensions, building rubrics for them, and deciding how much weight each one gets is a deeply clinical judgment. If engineers make those calls alone, they'll get them subtly wrong in ways that don't show up on benchmarks but show up in the real world.

So in practice I think there are a few distinct roles physicians play, and they shouldn't be collapsed into one.

The first is evaluation design. We work with a large network of practicing clinicians across specialties and across countries, and they help us build the evaluations, grade model outputs, and tell us where the model is being subtly unhelpful or unsafe. That's not a one-time thing. Every time the model's capabilities shift, the failure modes shift, and you need clinical eyes on the new behavior.

The second is in the training loop itself. Physicians help write and critique the data that shapes model behavior, so the model learns what a careful, thoughtful clinician would actually say, not what a textbook says. That includes the human parts, like how to talk to someone who's scared, or when to say "I don't know, you need to see someone in person."

The third, and this is the one people underrate, is having physicians embedded on the team with real decision-making authority. Not advisors you email once a quarter. People who sit in the research reviews, who can block a launch, who understand the model well enough to push back on the ML side and understand the clinic well enough to push back on the clinical side. The most valuable people I've worked with are the ones who straddle both worlds, and I think teams should actively invest in growing more of them.

The last thing I'd say is that physician expertise has to be paired with humility about what physicians don't know. A lot of health happens outside the exam room. Patients, caregivers, nurses, pharmacists, public health folks all see things doctors don't. The goal isn't to make the model think like a doctor. It's to make it genuinely useful for people navigating their health, and doctors are a critical input to that, but not the only one.

r001.rationale: The response describes an ongoing clinician network that helps build evaluations and gives feedback on model behavior, with clinical review recurring as capabilities change.

r002.rationale: It describes practicing clinicians contributing directly and physicians embedded on the team, but does not say close physician advisers synthesize broader community input for the team.

astra-6.text:
I think physicians need to be part of the research process from the beginning. You don’t want to build a system, hand it to a doctor at the end, and ask, “Is this good?” Clinical expertise should help determine which problems we work on, what information the model needs, and what a useful, safe response actually looks like.

That’s especially important for evaluation. A response can sound medically sophisticated and still miss the thing that would change a patient’s next step. Physicians can help us distinguish those consequential mistakes from less important ones, and design evaluations that reflect the ambiguity of real clinical practice.

I’d want a close partnership between clinicians and AI researchers, with practicing physicians bringing different specialties and settings into the conversation. The goal is a shared research process where clinical judgment shapes the experiments, and the results help us ask better clinical questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes physicians as partners throughout the research process, helping shape problems, experiments, and evaluations—not just completing a task at the end.

r002.rationale: It says physicians from different specialties and settings should participate, but does not describe close advisers synthesizing input from a broader physician community for the research team.

sol-6.1.text:
I think physicians need to be deeply integrated into the research process, from deciding which problems to work on to evaluating whether a model is actually useful. You don’t want to build something and then bring in a doctor at the end to tell you whether it makes sense.

There’s a lot of clinical judgment that isn’t captured by getting a medical exam question right. Did the model ask the right follow-up question? Did it recognize that it didn’t have enough information? Does its recommendation make sense given the patient’s circumstances? Physicians can help us identify those gaps and turn them into things we can study and improve.

And I’d want a range of perspectives—different specialties, different practice settings—because there isn’t one universal clinical workflow. The goal is a close collaboration where clinicians help shape the research and researchers help translate that expertise into better models and better evaluations.

r001.rationale: The response describes physicians as deeply integrated throughout the research process and as close collaborators who help shape research and evaluations.

r002.rationale: It calls for perspectives across specialties and practice settings, but does not say that physician advisers synthesize input from the broader physician community for the team.
